Washington, Oct. 5.—Anthracite will be scarce and difficult to obtain in large quantities for a long time after the resumption of work in the mines, according to the opinion of Dr. David T. Day, chief of the division of mines and mineral resources of the United States Geological Survey. Dr. Day, who is the best informed man in the government service as to the coal resources of the country, has been frequently called to the White House for consultation since President Roosevelt began his efforts to settle the strike.

In his opinion, if the strikers should all return to work tomorrow, and if the mines should be worked to their utmost capacity, working men in shifts, it would be at least six months before the supply of anthracite would bear a normal relation to the demand. In discussing this subject Dr. Day pointed out that the annual output of the anthracite mines of Pennsylvania was sixty million tons, or about five million tons a month. The demand is fully up to this supply that in normal times very large surplus stocks of coal can be accumulated, and now after an almost total stoppage of production of four months, there is practically no supply on hand. Domestic bins are empty, the sheds of the coal yards have been swept clean, and every ton in the producing region has been shipped to market. The season of the year in which the consumption of coal is greatest is setting in, and even if the mines could begin turning out coal at once at the rate of five million tons a month they would not keep pace with the normal demand for consumption during the winter months in the face of the fact that there is no surplus left over from the summer to draw on this year.

The mines could not at once resume their normal rate of production. Many of them have been flooded and damaged by water to such an extent that it would be several weeks before they could be put in full operation. At other mines buildings have been burned and machinery destroyed or damaged, and much time would be lost in starting them again. In view of these conditions every day's delay in starting the mines, with winter setting in, increases the danger of suffering and death among the poorer people and of great inconvenience and discomfort among the well-to-do. If the mines can be started at a reasonably early date it is believed that the prevention of distress will depend largely upon the management of the coal producing companies and the retail dealers.

The companies have said that they will not increase the price of coal and if the dealers will limit the amount sold to a single customer to his immediate needs, as is proposed to be done in Washington, it is believed the winter can be passed without severe hardships, on the assumption that the mines are soon to be started. If they are not, reliance will have to be placed on substitutes for anthracite. Dr. Day is disposed to believe that the chief reliance will have to be on bituminous coal and that the principal source of supply will be the bituminous mines of the United States with some little assistance from foreign fields. He says that the supply of Welsh anthracite is so small that not more than 4,000 or 10,000 tons of that coal could be imported annually without running the prices to a prohibitory figure, and that the amount that could be brought in at once would not be an appreciable factor in meeting the present demands.

Wood can be used only to limited extent, as few houses have facilities for wood fires. Oil and gas can be extensively used for cooking purposes and are being used in this way on a scale never approached before, but oil and gas heaters have not generally been found adequate and Dr. Day does not expect that they will be extensively used.
